introduction_markdown: CAMEROON GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2020, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 755 Geology 1'; fill in the information required on the answer sheet using your HB pencil (Candidate Name, Exam Session, Subject Code and Candidate Identification Number). Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why is granite not commonly used as an aggregate for road construction?

*Options as printed:* A) It has a high compressive strength   B) It is coarse grained   C) It is expensive to quarry   D) It has a low compressive strength
questions.corrige_markdown:
A road aggregate must be tough, hard-wearing and resistant to polishing. Granite has a **high** compressive strength, so options A and D cannot explain why it is rarely chosen (D is also false). The usual reasons are its coarse crystalline texture: a coarse-grained rock tends to break along the boundaries of large crystals, weathers along feldspar cleavages and gives less tough, less angular chips than fine-grained rocks such as basalt or dolerite, which are the preferred road aggregates. Cost of quarrying (option C) is possible for any hard rock, but the texture argument is the one given in textbooks.

**Intended answer: B (It is coarse grained).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 1), which shows the approximate mineral composition of igneous rocks, to answer questions 2, 3 and 4.

Name the two plagioclase minerals that would occur in A and in C respectively.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Column A has quartz, orthoclase and biotite: it is an acid rock (granite). Plagioclase in acid rocks is the sodium-rich end of the series, **albite** (or albite-oligoclase). Column C has plagioclase and augite with no quartz: it is a basic rock (gabbro or basalt), in which plagioclase is calcium-rich, typically **labradorite** (about An50-70). Only option B pairs a sodic plagioclase for A with a calcic one for C. Option A reverses the order (anorthite is the most calcic member) and options C and D use andesine, an intermediate member (printed 'Andesite', the name of a rock), which is typical of intermediate rocks, not of acid and basic ones.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 1) to answer this question as well.

Which mineral has the lowest density?

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Typical densities: orthoclase about 2.56 g/cm3, quartz about 2.65, biotite about 2.8-3.2, hornblende about 3.0-3.4. The light-coloured (felsic) minerals are less dense than the dark ferromagnesian ones, and orthoclase is lighter than quartz. The lowest density is that of orthoclase.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 1) to answer this question as well.

The most easily weathered mineral would be:

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Goldich's weathering series is the Bowen reaction series in the same order: the minerals that crystallise first at high temperature (olivine, then pyroxene) are the farthest from equilibrium with surface conditions and weather fastest, while quartz, crystallised last, is the most stable. Of the four options, olivine is weathered most easily.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 is a field sketch which a student did not have time to label completely. Use the sketch to answer questions 5 and 6.

Name the features labelled M and O respectively.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
M is the inclined line that cuts across all the beds and displaces them: it is a **fault** (a dyke or vein would be a filled, wider body). O is a lens in which thin laminae are inclined to the main bedding surface, which is **cross bedding** (cross lamination). A spring line is a groundwater feature on a hillside, not a structure seen in a quarry face. Answer B.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the sketch of figure 2 (the same figure as for question 5) to answer this question.

In which environment was the feature N formed?

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Options as printed:* A) Shallow marine   B) Deep marine   C) Desert   D) Lagoonal
questions.corrige_markdown:
N is the magnified view of one bed, drawn as a band of grains that changes in size from the base to the top, with thin parallel laminae in the bed. That is the signature of **graded bedding**, deposited when a turbidity current slows down and drops its coarsest grains first. Turbidites are typical of the continental slope and the deep marine basin. The intended answer is therefore deep marine. The drawing is too small to be sure of the grain-size trend, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Deep marine).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: From the jumbled list of rocks below, select the most likely sequence to show the formation of a gneiss from a granite:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sequence must pass through the surface (weathering, erosion, deposition) and then through increasing metamorphic grade. Granite weathers to clay (feldspar and mica break down to clay minerals) and sand (quartz). The clay is compacted to mudstone and shale; low-grade metamorphism turns it into **slate**, medium grade into **schist**, and high grade into **gneiss**. Option D follows this order. In B gravel would become a conglomerate (metaconglomerate), not slate; A skips the intermediate grades and C goes from clay straight to gneiss.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the information presented below to answer questions 8 and 9.

- Specimen K reacts with dilute HCl and forms cleavage rhombs.
- Specimen L is pink in colour, has a hardness of 6 and cleaves in 2 directions at 90 degrees.

Identify specimens K and L respectively.
questions.corrige_markdown:
K effervesces in cold dilute hydrochloric acid and splits into rhombohedra: the mineral **calcite** (limestone and marble are rocks, not specimens of a single mineral with cleavage rhombs). L is pink, has Mohs hardness 6 and two cleavages at 90 degrees: **orthoclase** feldspar (albite is white and its cleavages are at about 86 degrees). Answer B.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the information presented below to answer questions 8 and 9.

- Specimen K reacts with dilute HCl and forms cleavage rhombs.
- Specimen L is pink in colour, has a hardness of 6 and cleaves in 2 directions at 90 degrees.

What type of twinning is exhibited by specimen L?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Specimen L is orthoclase (question 8). Orthoclase characteristically shows simple contact or penetration twins of the **Carlsbad** type (two individuals joined along a plane, each half of the crystal reversed). Repeated (polysynthetic) twinning is typical of plagioclase (albite law), butterfly twins of calcite and geniculate (knee-shaped) twins of rutile and cassiterite.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (figure 3) depicts volcanic activities. Use it to answer questions 10 and 11.

The texture of rocks formed at K and L will respectively be:

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Options as printed:* A) Fine grained and coarse grained   B) Fine grained and medium grained   C) Glassy and fine grained   D) Medium grained and coarse grained
questions.corrige_markdown:
K is a body that reached the surface and spread along it: a lava flow, which cools quickly and is **fine grained** (glassy at the very top). L is a lens-shaped intrusion at moderate depth, a laccolith (question 11): a shallow (hypabyssal) body cools more slowly than a lava flow, giving a **medium-grained** (often porphyritic) texture; only a deep-seated pluton is coarse grained. Options A and B both start with fine grained at K, so the key depends on how deep L is judged to be: both are defensible, so the question is left open. Intended answer: fine grained at K, medium grained at L.

**Intended answer: B (Fine grained and medium grained).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 3), which depicts volcanic activities, to answer this question as well.

The igneous body L is:

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
L is a concordant intrusion with a flat base and a convex upper surface, fed from below by a narrow feeder: that is a **laccolith** (mushroom or lens shaped, doming the strata above). A phacolith occupies the crest or trough of a fold, which is not shown here; a lopolith is saucer shaped with a concave top; a dome is not an igneous body.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 below shows a photograph of a fossil.

Identify the fossil in the photograph.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The photograph shows elongate, slender stipes with a regular serrated edge (the thecae in a row), lying on a dark shale. These are the colonial hemichordates called **graptolites** (rhabdosomes). Trilobites show a segmented body with cephalon and pygidium; leaves show a midrib and veins; fish fins have fin rays.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A geology student studying a crystal model realizes that it has two planes of symmetry and an axis of two-fold symmetry.

To which system does the model belong?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A monoclinic crystal has at most one plane and one diad axis. A tetragonal crystal has a four-fold axis and a hexagonal crystal a six-fold axis. Two planes of symmetry that intersect in a two-fold axis (the line of intersection) characterise the **orthorhombic** system (for example the pyramidal class, with 2 planes and 1 diad axis). Answer B.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (figure 5) depicts a map. Use it to answer questions 14 and 15.

Identify the type of fault shown on the map.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Options as printed:* A) Normal fault   B) Reverse fault   C) Tear fault   D) Thrust fault
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the map the fault is a straight line that crosses the strike of the beds obliquely. Each band (conglomerate, shale, sandstone) is cut by it and is found again on the other side shifted sideways in the same direction, by roughly the same horizontal distance, without any change in the pattern of the beds: the movement was horizontal along the fault. Such a lateral shift is typical of a **tear (strike-slip) fault**. A straight trace across the map also indicates a nearly vertical fault plane. Because normal, reverse and thrust faults can also shift outcrops of dipping beds, and because the map gives no way to check the direction of throw, the question is left open. Intended answer: tear fault.

**Intended answer: C (Tear fault).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the map (figure 5) to answer this question as well.

Identify the folded feature on the map.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The dip symbols show the direction in which the beds slope down. On the west of the map the beds dip towards the east (30 and 50 degrees) and on the east of the map the beds dip towards the west (32 degrees): the limbs dip towards each other, with the same bands repeated symmetrically on either side of the central valley. Limbs that dip towards a common axis form a **syncline**. 'Antiformal syncline' and 'synformal anticline' describe refolded or overturned structures, which the map does not show. The interpretation relies on the dip arrows, which are small, so it is of moderate confidence.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 6) of two fossil trilobites W and X to answer questions 16 and 17.

What term is used to describe the relationship between the pygidium and the cephalon in fossil W?

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The size of the pygidium relative to the cephalon is described by: macropygous (pygidium larger than the cephalon), isopygous (about equal), mesopygous (smaller) and micropygous (very small). In W the tail shield has about the same width and length as the head shield, so it is **isopygous**.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 6) of two fossil trilobites W and X to answer this question as well.

State the mode of life of fossil X.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fossil X has a globular glabella, long curved genal spines and very long pleural spines, a narrow thorax and a spiny pygidium. These spines increase the surface area and hold the animal up in the water: such spiny trilobites are interpreted as free-floating or **swimming** (pelagic) forms. Burrowers (for example Asaphus) have smooth, streamlined bodies; crawlers have a flattened body with a broad exoskeleton; there were no boring trilobites. The reading is of moderate confidence because spiny trilobites are sometimes interpreted as bottom-living crawlers.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Fracture cleavage is formed by:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fracture cleavage is a set of closely spaced, parallel fractures that cut the rock, especially in competent rocks such as sandstone; the rock splits along them. The other options describe other kinds of cleavage: A is the mechanism of crenulation cleavage, B is the streaking-out of fold limbs in a strain-slip or differentiated cleavage and C is slaty cleavage (alignment of platy grains).

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Microscopic wrinkling of materials between cleavage planes
Streaked out limbs of microscopic folds
Microscopic grains lying in parallel planes

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram above (figure 7), which represents weathering of granites and peridotite, to answer questions 19 and 20.

Name the products formed at X and Y respectively.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
At X (weathering of granite) the alkalis and alkaline earths (K, Na, Ca, Mg) are leached away and the aluminium-rich residue at the surface is **bauxite**, the ore of aluminium. At Y (weathering of peridotite) the profile is capped by an iron oxide layer and iron-rich **laterite**; the nickel is concentrated lower in the altered peridotite. Option B reverses the products, option D names the profile layers, not products, and option A names the metal found in the lower part of the profile at Y, not the main product.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 7) to answer this question as well.

What name is given to the type of ore bodies formed when a rock like peridotite is weathered?

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
When a rock is weathered under warm, wet conditions the soluble constituents are removed and the insoluble useful material stays where it formed: this gives a **residual ore deposit** (nickel laterite from peridotite, bauxite from granite). A secondary (supergene) enrichment deposit forms when metals are dissolved from above and re-precipitated below the water table; chemical deposits form by precipitation from solution and detrital deposits from transport of grains (placers).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (figure 8) shows the variations in velocity of P and S waves within the Earth's interior. Use the diagram to answer questions 21 and 22.

Which layers of the Earth correspond to B and C respectively?

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The S-wave curve stops at about 2900 km (the Gutenberg discontinuity) because S waves cannot cross a liquid, and the P-wave velocity drops sharply there. B lies between about 2900 km and about 4800 km: this is the **outer core**. C is the thin interval below B where the P-wave velocity increases, the transition at about 5150 km marked by the **Lehmann discontinuity** (outer core to inner core). The Gutenberg discontinuity is the top of B, not C, so options C and D are wrong, and the mantle (option A) is above 2900 km.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 8) to answer this question as well.

What is the state of the layer D?

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
D lies below the Lehmann discontinuity: it is the inner core. Its P-wave velocity is higher than in the outer core and it transmits S waves (generated by conversion), and the very high pressure keeps the nickel-iron alloy **solid**. 'Nickel and iron' (D) is the composition, not the state.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram (figure 9) is a thin section of a sedimentary rock. Answer questions 23 and 24 using the diagram.

Which description best suits the degree of sorting of the rock?

![fig-9](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Sorting describes how uniform the grain size is. The thin section shows grains of very different sizes (from tiny to several millimetres) with angular outlines set in a fine clay matrix: the rock is **poorly sorted**. Options A and D describe the composition and texture, not the sorting, and C wrongly says moderately sorted.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Coarse angular fragments in a clay matrix
Moderately sorted with resistant quartz minerals
Angular fragments with rock fragments and clay matrix

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the thin section (figure 9) to answer this question as well.

Name this rock.

![fig-9](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rock contains angular quartz and rock fragments in more than 15 percent clay matrix and is poorly sorted: this is a **greywacke** (a 'wacke', an immature sandstone). A lithic sandstone or arenite has little matrix (clean, well sorted grains) and 'clastic sandstone' is not a specific name.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
What evidence would a shell of a bivalve have which shows that it was a borer?

*Options as printed:* A) Thick shell   B) Equal muscle scars and entire pallial line   C) Thick shell which is sharp   D) Thin shell with a pallial sinus
questions.corrige_markdown:
Rock-boring and wood-boring bivalves (for example Pholas, Lithophaga) excavate their burrows by rasping with the front of the shell, which is therefore sharp-edged, ridged and often thick or strongly sculptured. A pallial sinus (D) is the sign of a deep burrower with long siphons, a plain thick shell (A) says nothing about boring, and equal muscle scars with an entire pallial line (B) mark shallow, surface-living forms. The intended answer is the sharp, rasping shell, but the options are weakly worded, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: C (Thick shell which is sharp).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram (figure 10), which shows the internal view of the pedicle valve of a brachiopod, and use it to answer questions 26 and 27.

Which of the parts labelled W, X, Y and Z is the adductor muscle scar?

![fig-10](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the pedicle valve the muscle field lies in the middle of the valve. The narrow central scar, divided by a median line and flanked by the larger diductor scars, is the **adductor** scar (W). Y marks one of the lateral scars (diductors), X is the triangular opening beneath the beak, and Z is at the beak itself. The label lines are thin and the muscle scars are small in the printed figure, so the reading is of moderate confidence.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 10) to answer this question as well.

State the function of X.

![fig-10](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
X marks the triangular opening below the beak of the pedicle valve (the delthyrium), through which the fleshy stalk, the **pedicle**, passes to attach the animal to the sea floor. A brachiopod has no foot, the lophophore lies inside the shell and the valves are joined along the hinge line, which is a different structure.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (figure 11) illustrates the collision between the South American and Nazca plates. Use the diagram to answer questions 28 and 29.

Give the name of the feature labelled M.

![fig-11](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
M is a ridge on the ocean floor, directly above rising asthenosphere, with new lithosphere forming on either side: this is a mid-oceanic ridge, here the **East Pacific Ridge (East Pacific Rise)**, the divergent boundary at which the Nazca plate is created and from which it moves east towards South America. A seamount is an isolated volcano, a barrier reef is a coral feature and a hot spot plume is a rising column that does not form a ridge.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 11) to answer this question as well.

What type of rock is common in P?

![fig-11](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
P is a volcano on the continental edge above the subducting Nazca plate (the Andes). The melting of the subducted slab and the overlying mantle wedge gives magma of intermediate composition, which erupts as **andesite**, the typical rock of continental-margin volcanic arcs. Basalt is typical of ocean ridges, and granite and granodiorite are plutonic (intrusive) rocks, not those of a volcano.

**Answer: B.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: What term is applied to non-economic minerals found in hydrothermal deposits?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In an ore deposit the useful minerals are the ore minerals; the valueless minerals that occur with them (quartz, calcite, fluorite) are called **gangue minerals**. 'Tenor' is the metal content of an ore, and 'vein minerals' describes where the minerals occur, not whether they are economic.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A bed dips to the North. What is the strike direction of this bed?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The strike is the direction of a horizontal line on the bed and is always at 90 degrees to the direction of dip. A bed dipping north has a strike running east-west: **East to West**.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the block diagrams below (figure 12) and answer questions 32 and 33.

Name the type of folds represented by X and Y respectively.

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

*Options as printed:* A) Both folds are asymmetrical anticlines   B) Both folds are symmetrical anticlines   C) X is a syncline while Y is an asymmetrical anticline   D) X is an asymmetrical anticline while Y is asymmetrical anticline
questions.corrige_markdown:
In both blocks the oldest rocks (blank and circled layers) lie in the core of the arch and the youngest rocks (stipple) on the outside, so both folds are **anticlines** (rules out C). In block X the limbs have unequal dips (steep on one side, gentler on the other), so it is an asymmetrical anticline; the arch in block Y is closer to symmetrical, with limbs dipping at similar angles. As printed, options A and D say the same thing and B contradicts the shape of X, so the key is not reliable (option D seems to have lost a word such as 'a symmetrical'). The question is therefore left open. Intended answer: X an asymmetrical anticline, Y a (nearly) symmetrical anticline.

**Intended answer: D (X is an asymmetrical anticline while Y is asymmetrical anticline).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the block diagrams (figure 12) to answer this question as well.

On which side of the fault plane in diagram X is the downthrown side found?

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

*Options as printed:* A) North   B) South   C) East   D) West
questions.corrige_markdown:
The downthrown side is the side on which younger beds are brought to the present surface. On the top face of diagram X, the strip on the far (north) side of the fault line shows the youngest layer (stipple) wrapping around the nose of the fold, while the near side exposes older beds in the core. The north arrow points towards the back of the block, so the **north** side is the downthrown side. This reading depends on the orientation of the small north arrow and on the position of the fault line, both hard to read on the scan, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (North).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagrams below (figure 13) show structures produced during rock deformation. Use the diagrams to answer questions 34 and 35.

Name the structures M and N respectively.

![fig-13](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
M shows short, parallel cracks opening at the outer arc of a bent layer: these are **tension gashes** (tension fractures that may later be filled with minerals). N shows a competent layer stretched and broken into sausage-shaped blocks separated by pinched necks inside less competent material: this is **boudinage**. A mullion is a corrugation on a fold surface, not separated blocks.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagrams (figure 13) to answer this question as well.

These two structures were produced by:

![fig-13](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both tension gashes and boudinage are extension structures: the rock is pulled apart or stretched along the direction of the greatest extension, so they are produced by **tensional forces** (stretching).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Sedimentary rocks such as halite and gypsum which form due to evaporation of water are identified as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Halite (rock salt) and gypsum are evaporites: they crystallise directly from solution when the water evaporates, so they are **chemical** sedimentary rocks. Organic and biochemical rocks form from living organisms (coal, some limestones) and clastic rocks from fragments of older rocks.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Shallow focus earthquakes are common in:

*Options as printed:* A) Convergent plate boundary   B) Divergent plate boundary   C) Conservative plate boundary   D) Triple junction
questions.corrige_markdown:
Shallow-focus earthquakes (focus less than about 70 km) occur at every plate boundary, but at divergent (constructive) boundaries, where the lithosphere is thin and hot, all earthquakes are shallow, and the same is true on conservative (transform) boundaries. Convergent boundaries also produce intermediate and deep foci along the subducting slab. The intended answer is the divergent boundary, but the conservative boundary is equally defensible, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Divergent plate boundary).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
The triangular diagram below (figure 14) illustrates the primary types of mass movements: slide, flow and heave. Answer questions 38 and 39 using the diagram.

Which of these mass movements represents soil creep?

![fig-14](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_14.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Soil creep is the very slow, dry movement of soil caused by repeated expansion and contraction, called **heave**. On the triangle it plots near the Heave corner, in the slow, dry field: **Z**. W is near the Slide corner (fast, dry), X is near the Flow corner (fast, wet) and Y is the intermediate slow-flow field.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the triangular diagram (figure 14) to answer this question as well.

Which of these letters represents Solifluction?

![fig-14](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_14.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil, usually over frozen ground. It lies between the flow and heave corners, in the wet, slow field of the triangle: **Y**. X is the fast, wet field (mudflows), W the fast slide field and Z the heave (creep) field.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal model below (figure 15) and answer questions 40 and 41.

Name the forms X and Y respectively.

![fig-15](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_15.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The model is an octahedron whose corners are cut off by small square faces. The large triangular face Y belongs to the **octahedron** (eight equilateral-triangle faces); the small square face X, which truncates a corner, belongs to the **cube**. The crystal is therefore a combination of cube and octahedron.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the crystal model (figure 15) to answer this question as well.

Give the Miller Index of face X.

![fig-15](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_15.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
X is a cube face. A cube face cuts one crystallographic axis and is parallel to the other two: the intercepts are 1, infinity, infinity, so the reciprocals are 1, 0, 0 and the Miller index is **(100)**. The octahedron faces such as Y would be (111).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (figure 16) illustrates a section of the earth's crust and part of the mantle. Use this diagram to answer questions 42, 43 and 44.

What is the approximate thickness of C?

![fig-16](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_16.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
C is the double arrow that ends on the dashed line A. Reading the depth axis at the level of A gives about 22 km (measured on the figure: 0 km at the ocean surface, 40 km at the bottom, A at about 22 km), so the approximate thickness of the layer C is **20 km**. The arrow starts above the zero of the axis because the continent rises above sea level, so measuring the whole arrow gives about 31 km; the intended reading is the depth of A on the axis. 35 km is the average thickness of the whole continental crust and matches the lower dashed line B, not C.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 16) to answer this question as well.

What is the composition of the lower crust?

![fig-16](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_16.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The upper continental crust (sial) is granitic; the lower crust, below the Conrad discontinuity, is denser and **basaltic** in composition (sima, mafic rocks). Peridotite is the rock of the mantle.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram (figure 16) to answer this question as well.

Name the discontinuities that occur at A and B respectively.

![fig-16](gce-al-geology-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_16.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Going down from the surface the discontinuities are met in this order: the **Conrad** discontinuity (between the granitic upper crust and the basaltic lower crust, about 15-25 km deep) and then the **Mohorovicic** discontinuity (the base of the crust, about 30-40 km deep under continents). A is the shallower dashed line, so A is Conrad and B, the deeper one, is Mohorovicic. The Gutenberg (2900 km) and Lehmann (5150 km) discontinuities are in the core region, not in the top 40 km. The labels 'Lower crust' and 'Mantle' on the sketch are loosely placed, so the identification relies on the order of the two lines.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The nebular hypothesis suggests that the Solar System:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The nebular hypothesis (Kant and Laplace) states that the Sun and planets formed from a single, enormous rotating cloud (nebula) of gas and dust that contracted, flattened into a disc and condensed. It therefore proposes a single origin, and the cloud was mostly hydrogen and helium, not oxygen.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Evolved from an enormous rotating cloud
Formed from materials made up mostly of oxygen
Is the remnant of another solar system

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is often not a point source of pollution?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A point source comes from one identifiable location: a factory discharge pipe, a landfill site or a single oil spill. **Run off** (water flowing over farmland, roads and towns and carrying fertilisers, pesticides and oil) comes from a wide area and is a non-point (diffuse) source.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What type of life forms characterized the Mesozoic?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Mesozoic (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous) is the 'age of reptiles': dinosaurs and other egg-laying reptiles dominated, the first small mammals appeared, and gymnosperms (seed-bearing plants such as conifers and cycads) dominated the vegetation. Option A describes the Precambrian, B the early Palaeozoic and D the Cenozoic.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Primitive plants, bacteria algae, soft - bodied organisms
Shelled ocean dwelling organisms, armoured and bony fishes
Small mammals, egg laying reptiles and seed bearing plants
Large and small mammals, flowering plants

questions.enonce_markdown: Cassiterite is the principal ore of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cassiterite is tin oxide, SnO2, and is the principal ore of **tin**. Iron ores include haematite and magnetite, copper ores chalcopyrite, and aluminium is obtained from bauxite.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following can be classified as a derived fossil in Cretaceous rocks?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A derived fossil is a fossil that has been eroded from older rock and re-deposited in a younger one. Micraster (echinoid) and ammonites lived in the Cretaceous itself, and scleractinian corals appeared in the Triassic and live today. The **tabulate corals** died out at the end of the Palaeozoic (Permian), so any found in Cretaceous rocks must have been derived from older strata.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is the largest unit of geologic time?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The geological time scale is divided, from the largest unit to the smallest, into eons, eras, periods and epochs. The largest unit in the list is the **eon** (Phanerozoic, Proterozoic...).

**Answer: B.**
